title: Targeted search: finding the clients that fit your service for Flat-pack and fixture installation
audience: Flat-pack and fixture installation owners who want more repeat work from property managers, holiday rental managers, real estate offices and small offices in their service area.
learningOutcomes: Build a prospect list scored against written fit criteria for service area, visit size and repeat need
Identify public signals that a fit-out or furnishing need is starting, and explain why each one is a reasonable reason to make contact
Write a first approach that makes one specific, verifiable observation, offers one small next step and can be declined easily

instruction.heading: Decide what work you want before you look for it
instruction.body: Write down the flat-pack and fixture work you do well, such as furnishing and fixing rental units between tenancies, the suburbs you can reach without losing money on travel, the visit size you can sustain, and how often each kind of client needs you. A regular round across several units on a route you already run is usually worth more than a single job across town. These criteria are the filter for everything that follows.

instruction.heading: Build a scored prospect list
instruction.body: Keep every candidate in one list with a fit column, a status column, a source and a date added. Score each as strong fit, possible fit or not a fit. Ask whether the prospect sits inside your service area, whether it has a repeat need for small assembly or fixing work, whether you can reach the decision-maker, and whether the work sits inside your licence and insurance. Property managers with several units, holiday rental managers, real estate offices, small offices and childcare or aged care facilities are candidates to test. The research did not find evidence of how often these groups buy flat-pack or fixture work, so treat each group as a hypothesis. Use only business contact details published for business use. A business address is not automatically open to marketing.

instruction.heading: Watch public signals
instruction.body: In Victoria, Buying for Victoria lists current and past tenders, lets suppliers set alerts, and publishes each agency's annual plan. AusTender does the same for federal work. A public tender for minor works or fit-out at a community facility is a signal a business can respond to through the stated process. A council planning permit register may show a commercial fit-out at application stage. Use signals to decide when to contact a business or public body. Do not use address data to contact individual occupiers, and do not turn up at a home or a unit to make an offer.

instruction.heading: Make a first approach that is specific and easy to decline
instruction.body: A useful first message says how you came to know about the need, makes one observation that you can verify from a public notice or the business's own material, and offers one small next step, such as a written quote for a defined list of items or a fifteen-minute call. The ACCC's July 2026 release on unsolicited selling reported many pressured or misleading approaches, and that about 71 per cent of salespeople identified themselves. An honest, named approach stands out.

instruction.heading: Follow up on a fixed schedule and stop when asked
instruction.body: Decide the follow-ups in advance. One reminder after a week and one final message two weeks later, then a pause, is a common pattern. If a prospect says no or asks you to stop, remove them at once and record the date. Review each month which fit tier and which signal produced paid work.

procedure: Write the flat-pack and fixture work, area, visit-size and repeat-need criteria for the work you want.
Build the prospect list and score each entry as strong fit, possible fit or not a fit, with a reason and a source.
Choose two or three public signals to watch and record the date each one is seen.
Write one first message for each fit tier, with a stated source, one verifiable observation and one small next step.
Check each message against the electronic message rules and the licence rules for the work before sending.
Send to strong-fit prospects first, then follow up on the fixed schedule.
Remove anyone who asks you to stop, and review the results at the end of the month.

workedExamples.situation: A flat-pack installer covers three suburbs in Victoria. A public tender for minor fit-out and fixing works at a community facility in one of them is posted on Buying for Victoria, with a closing date and a named contact for questions. The scenario is illustrative.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Should the installer respond, and what should the response contain?
workedExamples.reasoning: A published tender is a route the agency has opened, so responding through the stated process is appropriate. Before responding, the installer confirms the scope, his capacity and the deadline. He checks that the shelving and furniture items are inside his work, and he refers any electrical item, such as a light fitting, to a licensed electrician, because the research did not settle the Victorian licence position for those tasks. He does not contact individual staff through private contact details. His response names the tender, says how he found it, offers one defined list of items with a price basis, and asks one question about access. He does not pressure the agency.

equipmentAndPpe: Prospect list in a spreadsheet or notebook, with fit, status, source and date columns
Written fit criteria for service area, visit size and repeat need
Message templates checked against the electronic message rules
No PPE is needed for desk work; any site visit follows the site's own safety rules

commonErrors.error: Sending the same message to everyone on a broad list at once.
commonErrors.prevention: Score the list first, write one message for each fit tier, and start with the strong-fit tier.

commonErrors.error: Using a resident's private details to offer assembly work after seeing a building notice.
commonErrors.prevention: Use only contact details published for business use, or details the person has given you for this purpose.

commonErrors.error: Pitching electrical work that you are not licensed to do.
commonErrors.prevention: Check the licence and insurance before outreach, and remove that work from the message.

commonErrors.error: Following up without a limit, or continuing after a request to stop.
commonErrors.prevention: Set a fixed number of follow-ups and a stop rule, and record every stop request.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Do not offer electrical or other licensed work in outreach unless you hold the licence the state where the work is done requires. The research did not settle which light-fitting or power-point tasks need a licence in any state. This lesson does not grant any licence.

Commercial electronic messages, including email and text, are regulated by the Spam Act 2003 (Cth). ACMA's guidance says marketing messages need consent, that consent should be recorded, and that unsubscribe requests must be honoured within five working days. ACMA's Spam Act obligations page (last updated 28 March 2019) says publishing a business address does not by itself permit commercial messages. The Act text was not read for this lesson.

A public listing or public notice does not by itself permit contact about anything. If the Privacy Act applies to your business, the OAIC's direct-marketing guidance says public information is not exempt. Use only contact details published for business use, keep them secure, and stop when someone objects.

Telemarketing to numbers on the Do Not Call Register is limited to weekdays from 9 am to 8 pm and Saturdays from 9 am to 5 pm, and not on Sundays or public holidays. That is from a 2018 industry guide, so check for updates before calling.

qualityStandard: Every prospect on the list has a fit score, a reason for that score and a recorded source for its contact details.
Every first message contains one verifiable observation and one small, easy-to-decline next step.
No contact is made using private information, and every stop request is recorded and actioned.
documentationEvidence: Prospect list with fit score, reason, status, source and date added
Signal log with the date each public signal was seen
Stop-request record with the date it was actioned
summary: Define the flat-pack and fixture work you want first, then filter prospects against that definition.
Watch public signals, and never use private information to make contact.
Keep the first approach specific and easy to decline, and stop when asked.

knowledgeChecks.question: Which prospect should you contact first?
options: A one-off job well outside your service area, because it looks large
Any business with a website, because it probably spends money on services
A property manager with several units inside your service area that you already visit

knowledgeChecks.question: A public tender for minor fit-out works at a community facility is posted. What is the most appropriate first step?
options: Message the facility staff members at their private addresses
Respond through the tender process, after checking scope, capacity, deadline and licence needs
Turn up at the facility and start the work the same day

knowledgeChecks.question: Before you send a commercial email to a prospect, what should you do?
options: Ask the prospect to like your social media page first
Choose a fun subject line and keep the message short
Confirm the Spam Act 2003 requirements in current ACMA guidance before sending
